pool.prompt: A fiber route initiation package is submitted to the SHPO on Monday. The SHPO returns it on Friday citing a missing field photo log. When does the 30-day Section 106 review clock start?
choices: On Monday — when the package was originally submitted
On the date a complete resubmission (including the missing photo log) is received by the SHPO — an incomplete submission does not start the clock
On Friday — when the SHPO responded
The clock never resets regardless of completeness
pool.explanation: The Section 106 review clock starts when the SHPO receives a complete submission with adequate documentation to make a determination. An incomplete package (missing required elements like a field photo log) does not start the clock — it restarts only once the missing information is provided.

pool.prompt: The SHPO issues an adverse-effect finding for a new aerial fiber route that will be visible in the viewshed of a National Register-listed historic farmstead. What are the available resolution options?
choices: The project must stop entirely — an adverse-effect finding automatically ends the federal undertaking

The agency and consulting parties resolve the adverse effect through further consultation — options can include design modification (e.g., alternate route, undergrounding a segment, pole placement changes) or a Memorandum of Agreement documenting mitigation measures — the project is not automatically terminated
The applicant can simply pay a fee to the SHPO to waive the finding
Only the federal agency (not the SHPO or applicant) can propose resolution options
pool.explanation: An adverse-effect finding triggers further consultation to resolve the effect, not automatic project termination. Resolution can include project design changes to avoid or minimize the effect, or a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) among consulting parties documenting agreed mitigation — the process is collaborative among the agency, SHPO/THPO, and other consulting parties.

pool.prompt: For a BEAD-funded aerial fiber route, the area of potential effects (APE) would typically include which of the following?
choices: Only the land directly beneath the poles where construction crews will physically work

The geographic area within which the undertaking may directly or indirectly cause alterations to historic properties — for an aerial route this can include the viewshed around visually-sensitive historic properties, not just the physical construction footprint
Only properties formally listed on the National Register, regardless of distance from construction
A fixed 500-foot buffer applied identically to every project type
pool.explanation: The APE is defined functionally, not just as the physical construction footprint — it's the geographic area within which the undertaking may directly OR indirectly affect historic properties. For an aerial fiber route near a visually-sensitive historic property, the APE can extend to the relevant viewshed, since a new aerial line could constitute a visual/setting effect even without any ground disturbance at the historic property itself.

pool.prompt: In the Section 106 process, who can be identified as a consulting party beyond the SHPO and the lead federal agency?
choices: Only the SHPO and the federal agency are ever consulting parties — no one else

Local governments with jurisdiction over the affected area, the applicant for federal assistance/permit/approval, Indian tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations with interests in the area, and other individuals/organizations with a demonstrated interest in the undertaking's effects on historic properties
Only the property owner of the specific historic property in question
Only members of Congress representing the project's district
pool.explanation: Section 106 consulting parties extend well beyond the SHPO and federal agency: a local government with jurisdiction, the federal-assistance/permit applicant, tribes/NHOs with interests in the APE, and other parties with a demonstrated interest in the undertaking's historic-property effects can all be identified as consulting parties.

pool.prompt: Why does an incomplete Section 106 submission (e.g., a missing field photo log) create real schedule risk, rather than being a minor paperwork inconvenience?
choices: It doesn't create schedule risk — the SHPO always processes incomplete submissions on the original schedule

Because the 30-day review clock does not start until the SHPO has a complete submission — an incomplete first submission silently adds the full round-trip time (SHPO review, rejection notice, resubmission, and re-review) to the project schedule, which is avoidable with a complete-on-first-submission package
Because incomplete submissions are automatically escalated to a full EIS
Because the SHPO charges an additional fee for each resubmission
pool.explanation: Since the review clock only starts on a COMPLETE submission, an incomplete first package doesn't just delay the SHPO's initial response — it adds the entire round-trip (identify the gap, notify, resubmit, restart the clock) to the project timeline, which is why submitting complete documentation the first time is a genuine schedule-risk mitigation, not just administrative tidiness.

pool.prompt: A project team wants to define the APE for an aerial fiber route as narrowly as possible — just the physical pole-line corridor — to minimize the number of historic properties requiring evaluation. Is this a defensible approach under 36 CFR 800.16(d)?
choices: Yes — the APE is always limited to the physical construction footprint by regulatory definition

No — because the APE definition is functional (based on where the undertaking may directly OR indirectly affect historic properties, including visual/setting effects), artificially narrowing it to only the physical footprint risks omitting properties with a genuine viewshed or setting effect, which can surface as a deficiency later in review rather than resolving the issue
Yes, as long as the SHPO doesn't object during the initial 30-day window
No — the APE must always be defined as the entire county regardless of project scope
pool.explanation: Because the APE definition turns on where effects (direct or indirect, including visual/setting effects) may occur — not simply on where construction physically happens — artificially narrowing the APE to just the pole-line footprint risks omitting a historic property with a genuine viewshed effect. That omission doesn't make the effect disappear; it just risks surfacing as a deficiency or a later adverse-effect dispute rather than being addressed during the initial identification phase.

pool.prompt: A fiber project's Section 106 package lists only the SHPO and the federal lead agency as consulting parties, despite the route running through a city with a documented local historic-preservation commission and near land with tribal cultural significance. Is this consulting-party list complete?
choices: Yes — the SHPO and lead agency are the only parties Section 106 requires

No — a local government with jurisdiction over the affected area and a tribe/NHO with a demonstrated interest in the APE are both entitled to participate as consulting parties, and omitting them risks an incomplete Section 106 record
Yes, because tribes and local governments can only participate if they pay a formal application fee to join
No — but only because federal law requires a minimum of five consulting parties on every project
pool.explanation: Section 106's consulting-party provisions extend beyond the SHPO and federal agency to include a local government with jurisdiction and tribes/NHOs with a demonstrated interest in the APE — omitting parties who are entitled to participate risks both an incomplete administrative record and a later procedural challenge to the review.

pool.prompt: What is the practical relationship between a project's APE and the number of historic properties that must be evaluated in the Section 106 process?
choices: There is no relationship — the number of properties evaluated is fixed regardless of APE size

A larger, more accurately-scoped APE (including relevant viewshed/setting areas) means more historic properties fall within the review, which increases the identification workload but also reduces the risk of missing a property with a genuine effect that later surfaces as a compliance problem
A larger APE always eliminates the need for a photo log
The APE only affects which agency has jurisdiction, never which properties are evaluated
pool.explanation: The APE directly drives the scope of the historic-property identification effort — the tradeoff is between the upfront workload of evaluating more properties (correctly scoped APE) versus the downstream compliance risk of an artificially narrow APE that misses a property with a real effect, which is the core reason APE-scoping is treated as a consequential early decision rather than a formality.
